name: dirty-flag
intent: Defer recomputation of derived data until it is actually needed: a dirty flag records that the cached result is out of date when the primary data changes, so several changes collapse into one recomputation and data that did not change is never recomputed.
problem: Derived data is recomputed eagerly on every change of its inputs - and recomputed again on every read. When an object changes several times before its derived value is used, the intermediate recomputations are thrown away (in the canonical scene-graph example four local transforms change and one world transform is computed four times for a single render); when the value is cheap to keep but expensive to compute, recomputing on every access wastes work whenever nothing changed at all. The naive fixes both fail: eager recomputation costs time proportional to the number of changes rather than to the number of uses, and always-fresh computation costs time proportional to the number of reads.
context: Applies when a set of primary (source) data changes over time and a derived value produced from it by a costly process is needed less often than the primary data changes - and maintaining that value incrementally is hard. Typical settings: scene graphs and layout systems (world transforms, arrangement, painting), editors and persistence (unsaved-change indicators, dirty entities flushed by a unit of work), caches of expensive derivations (indexes, parsed forms, compiled plans, checksums, serialisations), and reactive UI state. In single-threaded code the decision is about cost and staleness; as soon as several threads can mutate the source or read the cache, the flag and the cached value must be published together, and that publication order is where the failure modes concentrate.
benefits: Collapses several changes into one recomputation: marking costs one store per mutation, so a batch of updates ends in a single recomputation at the next read instead of one recomputation per change.
Skips work that would never be used: an object that is removed, hidden or simply never queried never recomputes its derived value at all.
Skips recomputation for inputs that did not change - static geometry, untouched entities and unmodified documents answer reads with a flag test.
Decouples mutation time from computation time, so the deferred work can be moved to a frame boundary, a checkpoint, an idle callback or a background task instead of running inside every mutation.
Keeps the read path cheap while the cache is clean: one bit test plus the cached value, with no recomputation and, in the concurrent forms, no lock on the fast path.

Keeps the derived data an implementation detail: callers keep asking the same accessor and only the accessor knows that a cache exists, so the optimization can be removed again without touching clients.
tradeoffs: Correctness rests on an invariant no compiler enforces: every mutation path must set the flag, and a single missed path silently serves stale derived data - the classic cache-invalidation bug, whose symptom appears far away from its cause.

Deferring is not free at the moment of use: the recomputation is expensive by assumption, so the first read after a change can stall its caller (a frame hitch, a slow request), and when the deferred work is persistence a crash before the flush loses it - the unsaved-changes star in a title bar is a dirty flag, and auto-save exists to compensate for exactly this risk.
Memory is traded for speed: the derived data must stay resident and current-looking, which costs memory the compute-on-demand approach would not use.
The guard adds a branch (and one more memory read) to every access; on a hot path a mispredicted branch can cost more than the small computation it was meant to avoid.

Under concurrency the flag becomes part of the publication state: the cache and the cleared flag must become visible together (publish the cache first, then clear the flag with release/acquire semantics) or another thread observes a clean flag with a partially built or stale cache.

Granularity is a design decision with no default: fine-grained flags reduce wasted recomputation but add a bit and bookkeeping per unit plus more paths that must mark, while coarse flags save memory and bookkeeping and recompute large, mostly unchanged aggregates.

Debuggability suffers: the recomputation happens at a different time and place from the change that caused it, so reentrancy, error handling and cache ownership are harder to reason about than a straight call chain.

A plain volatile boolean is insufficient for cross-thread coordination: it does not guarantee memory visibility or ordering between threads, and does not couple the flag with the cached value atomically - a reader may observe a clean flag before the writer's cache write is visible, or see the new flag value with a stale cache.

Using AtomicBoolean alone does not guarantee coherence between the flag and the cached value: IsDirty() and the array write in the same function are not atomic together - both the flag and the data it guards must be updated inside the same critical section.

participants.responsibility: The source state that changes over time (a transform, entity fields, document text) and the only state mutations are allowed to touch directly.
The expensive computed value (world transform, layout, index, serialisation) cached until invalidated; correct only while the flag is clear.
One bit per cache - or the absence of a cache slot - recording that the primary data has changed since the derived data was last computed.
Every operation that changes primary data; responsible for setting the flag, ideally through one narrow API so the invariant cannot be missed.
The read path: if the flag is set it runs the expensive process, publishes the new derived data and clears the flag; otherwise it returns the cached value.

use_cases: Scene graphs and render trees: world transforms, bounding volumes and skinning matrices cached per node, invalidated when a local transform changes and propagated through the traversal instead of recursively marking children.
Editors and documents: the unsaved-changes indicator and the save-on-close behaviour are a dirty flag over the file on disk, and auto-save is the compensating mechanism for deferring the flush.

Persistence change tracking: an ORM or unit of work marks an entity dirty when a mapped property changes and flushes only the dirty entities at commit (JPA/Hibernate dirty checking, EF Core change tracking).
Layout and drawing frameworks: browsers and UI toolkits keep dirty bits for style, layout and paint so that a property change schedules only the affected subtree for recomputation.
Caches of expensive derivations that are read far more often than their source changes: search indexes, parsed syntax trees, compiled plans, checksums and serialised payloads.
Physics and simulation: bodies at rest are clean and skipped until an impulse marks them dirty (the 'is moving' bit), the same flagging that sleeping/activation systems use.
Reactive UI state: a framework computed value tracks its dependencies and re-evaluates only when one of them changed - a dirty flag managed by the framework instead of by hand.

Change Data Capture (CDC) pipelines: Debezium monitors database binlog or WAL and streams row-level changes; each change record is a dirty notification emitted to Kafka where downstream consumers invalidate caches, rebuild search indexes, or update read replicas - Debezium's ExtractChangedRecordState SMT even emits per-field changed/unchanged headers, making the dirty flag explicit at field granularity.

Browser layout/paint invalidation: DOM mutation marks the layout tree dirty; the browser defers reflow and repaint to a separate style/layout/paint pass rather than running on every attribute change (the requestAnimationFrame batch is a dirty-flag flush).

Physics engine sleeping: bodies at rest are marked clean; an impulse marks the body dirty; the solver skips all clean bodies; velocity below a hysteresis threshold marks the body clean again - a self-resetting dirty flag with domain-specific clear semantics.

Noita-style dirty rectangles: falling-sand particle simulations track dirty bounding-rectangle regions; only particles inside dirty rects are scanned per frame, reducing checks from millions of particles to thousands within dirty regions (documented 23x reduction in particle checks per frame).
Unreal Engine's LOD and packet dirty flags: actors mark network state dirty for replication; the net driver flushes only dirty actor state over the wire rather than full state snapshots every frame.

Android view invalidation: View.invalidate() marks the view hierarchy dirty; the next Choreographer frame picks up dirty regions and issues only the necessary GPU draw calls - similar to browser paint invalidation.

Client-side form dirty tracking: per-field dirty sets distinguish user mutations (update) from programmatic initialisation (hydrate); 'isDirty' is derived from the dirty set size, so reverted fields are removed automatically and no extra bookkeeping is needed for reset scenarios.

CDC idempotent consumer: Debezium events carry LSN/offset provenance; downstream consumers track processed offsets per table in a separate state store to achieve idempotency even under at-least-once delivery - the processed-offset map is itself a dirty-flag tracking which records have been applied.

Multi-threaded computation cache: in a concurrent reader/writer model, an atomic TryConsumeDirty operation (compare-and-swap on the flag) ensures exactly one thread recomputes while others block or spin-wait, providing thread-safe lazy recomputation with no redundant work.

Unity Transform.hasChanged: the engine's built-in dirty flag - any operation touching a Transform sets it, whether or not the values actually differ, and parent changes flag the children too; Unity never clears it automatically, so consumers poll hasChanged and manually reset it to false to open a new detection window.

WPF layout system: InvalidateMeasure/InvalidateArrange mark an element's measure/arrange state invalid and the layout update happens asynchronously in one batched layout pass; the docs explicitly warn against forcing UpdateLayout after every small change, because forcing the flush defeats the deferral.

Chromium compositor (cc): two-stage dirty tracking separates invalidation (which layer regions must be re-rastered, Layer::SetNeedsDisplay) from damage (the visible difference between two CompositorFrames, computed by the DamageTracker); damage drives partial swaps so only the changed screen area is redrawn, saving GPU work and power.
avoid_when: The derived data is needed after almost every change: recompute eagerly (or maintain it incrementally), because the flag would be set on every mutation and the deferral buys nothing.

The derived data can be updated incrementally for less than the cost of a flag test: keep a running total instead of recomputing from scratch (add and subtract the item's weight rather than summing the hold).
The computation is cheap: a branch, a cached value and a second code path cost more than recomputing, especially when the branch mispredicts.
Freshness is a correctness requirement: safety, pricing, inventory or authorisation decisions that must reflect the latest write cannot tolerate a lazily refilled cache - read the source data.
The derived value is cheap to recompute but expensive to retain (a huge aggregate, streamed data): calculating on demand avoids keeping it in memory.
The deferred work must not be lost and there is no crash-safe consumer or checkpoint: making persistence lazy without auto-save or backup trades user data for performance.
A framework already tracks the dependencies (reactive computed values, immutable persistent structures with structural sharing, snapshot caches): use it instead of hand-rolling flags.

Hibernate PersistenceContext is large and contains many entities: the default O(n) dirty check scans every entity property; use bytecode-enhanced dirty tracking or a CustomEntityDirtinessStrategy, or consider splitting across multiple short-lived PC instances.

A framework already provides reactive computed values with automatic dependency tracking (MobX @computed, Vue computed, React useMemo with proper deps): hand-rolled dirty flags are redundant and introduce the cache-invalidation correctness risk that the framework already handles.

The domain naturally produces an audit log or event stream: event sourcing stores the delta (the change) rather than the snapshot, making the dirty-flag's derived state the source of truth rather than a cache - prefer event sourcing when audit/temporal queries are required.

Change Data Capture is already in the stack: if a Debezium/CDC pipeline is already streaming database changes to consumers, adding per-entity dirty flags duplicates the detection layer; CDC IS a dirty-flag system at the infrastructure boundary.

The team lacks the discipline to route every mutation through one choke point: without structural enforcement (a type system, a mutable struct with private fields, or a framework hook), a single unguarded mutation path will eventually introduce silent staleness.

Long-running transactions hold dirty entities in memory across user think time (e.g. wizard UIs with a single PersistenceContext): memory grows without bound and stale data accumulates; split into shorter sessions or use periodic EntityManager.clear() with explicit reattachment.
anti_patterns: Forgetting to mark on one mutation path: most update sites set the flag, one does not, and the program serves stale derived data - the classic cache-invalidation bug.

Clearing the flag before the new derived data is published, or clearing it when the recomputation failed: the cache is now considered clean while holding old or partial data, and nothing will ever recompute it again.
Recursively marking every dependent object dirty from a mutation: an O(n) walk on a hot mutation path replaces the O(1) mark; propagate dirtiness through the traversal that already visits them.
One coarse flag over a large aggregate so that any small change recomputes everything - or, symmetrically, a flag per element whose bookkeeping costs more than the recomputation it saves.
Exposing the flag or the cache as public API: callers start clearing flags, writing caches or branching on them, and the invariant can no longer be enforced in one place.
Treating one-shot lazy initialisation as invalidation: a null-check cache (or Lazy<T>, lazy val, OnceLock, kotlin lazy) is never re-run and cannot serve mutable primary data.

Guarding the flag with unsynchronised reads and writes across threads, or with double-checked locking that lacks volatile/atomic semantics, so a reader sees a clean flag or a partially constructed cache.

Using a volatile boolean alone for cross-thread dirty signalling without atomic coupling to the cached value: the flag signals intent, not state, and a torn or partially-ordered write/read makes the cache appear clean while containing stale data.

CDC idempotency gap: downstream consumers that do not track processed offsets per table will re-apply the same change event after a restart, producing duplicate database rows or incorrect aggregates - the processed-offset map must survive process restarts.
design_principles: Single source of truth: the derived data is a cache, never a second authoritative copy - only derived data is thrown away and rebuilt.
Encapsulation of an invariant: mutations go through one narrow API so that 'mark dirty' has exactly one home per type.
Lazy evaluation: perform the work at the latest point at which it is still useful, and only if it is needed at all.
Separation of concerns: the mutation path owns invalidation, the accessor owns recomputation, the cache owns storage - no role does another's job.
Measure before optimizing: a dirty flag is a targeted performance fix with a correctness risk, so introduce it only where the recomputation cost is measured and the change/read ratio favours it.
Optimization behind a stable interface: the accessor's contract (always a correct value) must not change when the cache is added, so the optimization remains removable.
Atomic coupling under concurrency: the flag and the cached value are one unit of publication - never update one without the other inside the same critical section or compound atomic operation.
best_practices: Set the flag in exactly one place per type - a property setter, a mutator method or an invalidate() helper - and route every mutation through it.
Start dirty: a newly created object has no valid cache, so the flag's initial state is set (or the cache slot starts empty).
Clear the flag only after the new derived value has been published and the recomputation returned successfully; under concurrency publish the cache first, then clear the flag.
Propagate dirtiness down an existing traversal (pass a parent-dirty argument into the child visit) instead of recursively marking children on every mutation.
Keep the flag and the cache private and expose only the accessor; never let callers branch on the flag.
Choose the granularity deliberately and document it: fine-grained flags pay bookkeeping per unit to avoid recomputing unchanged data, coarse flags do the opposite.
Bound the deferral: if the recomputation is long, run it at a checkpoint or in the background (with safe concurrent access to the primary data), or auto-save, rather than at an arbitrary read.
Keep the recomputation idempotent and free of side effects, since it can run at unpredictable times and must not itself mark the cache dirty.

For Hibernate: prefer bytecode-enhanced dirty tracking (build-time instrumentation via hibernate-enhance-maven-plugin with enableDirtyTracking=true) over the default diff-based snapshot comparison when the PersistenceContext holds many entities - avoids O(n) property-by-property reflection scans at flush time; the entity tracks its own dirty fields through $$_hibernate_tracker and $$_hibernate_trackChange.

For Hibernate extended PersistenceContext: be aware that the PC grows without bound as a first-level cache; use entity-manager-per-request or batch-flush patterns to prevent OutOfMemoryException; be mindful that stale data accumulates when the PC lives across user think time.

For EF Core: use the same DbContext instance to both query and update entities - EF Core automatically marks returned entities as Unchanged, property changes are detected at SaveChanges, and original values are preserved for efficient UPDATE statements; prefer this over manually managing entity state.

In Hibernate, implement CustomEntityDirtinessStrategy to plug in application-specific dirty detection (e.g. reading dirty fields from a hardware register, a network message, or a domain-event log) when the default mechanism is too expensive.

Adopt a dirty-rate metric (dirty queries / total queries): if >50%, the flag buys little and eager recomputation or a running-total approach is better; if <10%, the flag is highly effective - measure with a profiler before and after.

For physics/simulation sleeping: use an 'is moving' dirty flag per body; mark dirty on impulse, clear when velocity drops below a hysteresis threshold; sleeping bodies skip the solver entirely - this is the same dirty-flag structure but with domain-specific clear semantics.

For concurrent access: use compare-and-swap (CAS) on the dirty flag (e.g. Interlocked.CompareExchange, AtomicBool::compare_exchange) so that exactly one thread performs the recomputation; other threads block or spin-wait. Do not use a plain volatile boolean for cross-thread signalling - it does not couple the flag with the cache atomically.

For thread-safe recomputation: wrap both the flag check/clear and the cache write inside the same critical section (synchronized, ReentrantLock, or a compound CAS on a struct). Reading the flag and the cache in separate operations without ordering guarantees produces torn or stale data.

For form state: distinguish between hydrate() (programmatic init, establishes new pristine baseline without marking dirty) and update() (user mutation, marks the field dirty and adds it to the dirty set); 'isDirty' is the size of the dirty set, so fields that are mutated back to their initial value are removed from the set automatically.

For CDC idempotency: track processed LSN or offset per table in a durable store (a database table, not process memory) so that a consumer restart resumes without re-applying already-processed events; Debezium's at-least-once delivery guarantee requires an idempotent downstream sink.

For CDC schema evolution: use Debezium's ExpandContract migration pattern for non-breaking changes (add nullable fields, add fields with defaults); for breaking changes (column rename, type change), use a two-phase approach: add the new column alongside the old, migrate data, then drop the old column.

For Vulkan/Unreal-style scene graphs: store nodes in a flat array with stable indices (uint32_t parent_index) and topologically sort at load time so parents precede children; a single forward pass over the array propagates dirty status and recomputes world matrices with optimal cache locality.

For dirty-rectangle particle simulations (Noita-style): use two bounding rects - previous_frame_rect and current_delta_rect; union them for the render/update scan region, then assign current_delta_rect to previous_frame_rect and reset current_delta_rect for the next frame; a single growing rect that only expands will balloon to cover the entire world.

For CDC exactly-once idempotency: use upsert semantics (INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE) keyed on the event's source.lsn or source.position rather than a processed_flag column; store the processed offset per source partition in a durable topic (__debezium-connect-offsets) not process memory.

For thread-safe concurrent readers with one writer: prefer a ReentrantReadWriteLock - readers proceed without contention while the writer holds the exclusive lock; avoid Lock.stripAccumulator() pitfalls where stale reads can occur if the lock's internal state is not fully visible.

For Hibernate bytecode-enhanced dirty tracking: ensure your build tool runs hibernate-enhance-maven-plugin (or Gradle equivalent) with enableDirtyTracking=true; note that JPA @Entity annotation processing is a separate, unrelated mechanism that does NOT produce dirty tracking - these are frequently confused.

For EF Core high-throughput bulk operations: set ChangeTracker.AutoDetectChangesEnabled = false before a bulk import, then re-enable and call DetectChanges() once at the end; this avoids O(n) snapshot comparisons for each individual entity entry during the bulk phase.

For physics engine sleeping (dirty body flag): mark the rigid body dirty on impulse/collision; clear it when velocity magnitude stays below a hysteresis threshold for a cooldown period (e.g. 0.5 s); sleeping bodies are skipped by the solver entirely, saving CPU; the 'is awake' bit is the dirty flag with domain-specific clear semantics.

For MobX computed-to-manual-dirty-flag bridging: prefer keeping the computed observed by at least one reaction (use keepAlive=true) rather than adding a manual dirty flag wrapper, which reintroduces the cache-invalidation correctness risk the framework already handles safely.

For incremental computation: when the dirty-flag deferral cost is still too high (change/read ratio approaches 1), consider an incremental approach where the derived value is updated directly with the delta (e.g. sum += delta rather than recompute sum from scratch), trading O(1) update for O(1) recomputation.

'cc/' Compositor README — Two-stage dirty tracking in the Chromium compositor: invalidation marks which layer regions must be re-rastered (Layer::SetNeedsDisplay), damage is the visible difference between two CompositorFrames computed by the DamageTracker; damage enables partial swaps that redraw only the changed screen region.

Code With Karani. 'Your Redis Cache Is Serving Yesterday's Data: Fixing Invalidation Properly' (2026) — Misuse analysis of change-marking: invalidation code living in only one write path lets the other paths serve stale data silently, and TTL expiry masks the missing-mark bug instead of fixing it; prescribes one shared choke-point for keys, invalidation after transaction commit, and version counters - the same 'every mutation path must mark' invariant as the dirty flag.

Atomic Object (Spin). 'Caching: The Bad Parts' (2025) — Criticism of the caching/deferral family: keeping data fresh introduces eventual-consistency windows and complexity whose bugs can outweigh the latency saved - supporting the dirty-flag tradeoff that caches are only justified where recomputation cost is measured and the change/read ratio favours deferral.
